article.title: Beware big swings in midterm forecasts
article.subtitle: As Labor Day approaches, we’re entering the traditional stretch run of the campaign. But history says the national picture probably won’t change much…

extraction.summary: Model Talk arguing that the national environment rarely shifts much after Labor Day in modern midterms. Since 2010 the generic ballot moved 1.4 points on average from Labor Day to Election Day, less than the 2.1-point average final error, so most remaining uncertainty is polling error rather than drift. The piece explains why generic ballot averages need heavier smoothing than presidential averages, compares Silver Bulletin's smoother average with RealClearPolitics, and restates the goal of minimal autocorrelation in averages. It includes FLIPR's table translating popular-vote margin into House win probability and expected seats.

findings.statement: Since 2010, the Silver Bulletin generic ballot average has moved by an average of 1.4 points (absolute margin change) between Labor Day and Election Day; only in 2014 did it move by more than 2 points.

quantities.name: average Labor Day to Election Day generic ballot swing

findings.evidence_quote: On average in elections since 2010, the margin between Democrats and Republicans in our generic ballot average has swung by a whopping total of… 1.4 points between Labor Day and Election Day.

findings.statement: Since 2010 the average absolute error of the Labor Day generic ballot in predicting the national House popular vote is 3.5 points, falling to 2.1 points for the final generic ballot average. Because the 2.1-point Election Day error exceeds the 1.4-point drift, most remaining national uncertainty after Labor Day comes from polling error rather than opinion movement.
findings.evidence_quote: In terms of the national picture, most of the remaining uncertainty in the forecast stems from polling error rather than further movement in public opinion.

findings.statement: Historical generic ballot table (Democratic margin at Labor Day, on Election Day, and in the House popular vote): 2010 -5/-6/-7; 2014 Election Day -3, vote -6; 2018 +8/+8/+9; 2020 +8/+7/+3; 2022 Election Day -1, vote -3; 2024 Election Day 0, vote -3.

FLIPR's September 2026 seat-translation table gives Democratic House win probability and expected seats by popular-vote margin: D+0-1: 7.4 percent, 211 seats; D+2-3: 50.7 percent, 218; D+3-4: 77 percent, 221; D+4-5: 93.4 percent, 225; D+5-6: 98.9 percent, 229; D+6-7: 99.9 percent, 232; D+9-10: 245; D+14-15: 268. That is roughly 4 to 5 seats per point of popular vote. Democrats need about D+3 to be favored and D+4 to 5 for a double-digit majority.

quantities.name: D win prob at D+2 to +3

findings.statement: Silver Bulletin uses different smoothing parameters for different polling series. Generic ballot averages are smoothed heavily because Congress makes less national news, races are local, polling is spread over many races, and generic ballot polls are wording-sensitive and unherded (August 2026 polls ranged from D+11 Zogby to D+2 RMG). Presidential election averages and approval averages put a bigger premium on new data.

quantities.name: range of August 2026 generic ballot polls

findings.rationale: A polling model should not take a one-size-fits-all approach.
findings.evidence_quote: A polling model shouldn’t take a one-size-fits-all approach to calculate its averages.

findings.statement: The goal for polling averages is minimal autocorrelation in their changes: today's average should be the best prediction of the near-future average. If a decline would predictably bounce back, the average is overreacting; if it would predictably keep falling, it is underreacting.
findings.rationale: Learned from building averages that were both over- and under-responsive.
findings.evidence_quote: In technical terms, the goal is for changes in our polling averages to have as little autocorrelation as possible.

findings.statement: The RealClearPolitics generic ballot average, being under-smoothed, swung from D+8.1 in late May to D+4.7 by mid-July 2026, a 3.4-point drop that was mostly noise. The Silver Bulletin average, smoother and with a more comprehensive poll set, moved only 1.2 points (D+7.1 to D+5.9).
findings.evidence_quote: Because an under-smoothed average will overfit to small fluctuations in the data, a few days of bad polls can move the topline picture fairly dramatically.

findings.statement: In presidential years, swing-state polls can be used reliably to infer the national trend, since the same candidates appear everywhere. For congressional races, shifts in one race often reflect local news or an ad barrage and do not extrapolate well; a new Senate poll in one state mostly affects only that state.
findings.evidence_quote: A new poll in Michigan or Maine or South Carolina or Alaska pretty much affects that state and that state only.

findings.statement: Trends within a single pollster's series tell more than differences across pollsters, but they take more evidence and time to calibrate.
findings.evidence_quote: Trends within a given pollster’s data (i.e., if the New York Times/Siena College poll shows Republicans gaining ground on the generic ballot) tend to tell you more than trends across different pollsters

findings.statement: Uncontested House districts cause slight, predictable discrepancies between the generic ballot and the House popular vote; FLIPR corrects for these.
findings.evidence_quote: FLIPR corrects for these, but they’re minor enough that they can usually be treated as a rounding error.

findings.statement: A single outlier poll (Harvard-Harris R+2) plus other overnight polls moved the generic ballot from D+6.7 to D+6.4 and FLIPR's House odds from 84 to 81 percent, illustrating the model's damped response to individual polls.

political_insights.insight: The idea that voters only tune in after Labor Day is outdated; modern midterm environments change little after it.
political_insights.evidence: 1.4-point average post-Labor Day generic ballot movement since 2010.
political_insights.forecasting_implication: Shrink national drift variance in the fall of a midterm.
